title: In 1896 Ethiopia defeated an invading Italian army at Adwa
body: The war grew out of a treaty with two texts. In the Amharic version of the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale, Ethiopia *could* use Italy’s help in its foreign affairs; in the Italian version it was obliged to, which Italy used to claim a protectorate. Emperor Menelik II refused, and on **1 March 1896**, near Adwa, his army of between 73,000 and over 100,000 men, largely armed with modern rifles bought from France and Russia, overwhelmed an Italian force of under 20,000. Italy then signed the Treaty of Addis Ababa recognising Ethiopia’s independence.

left.label: Amharic version
left.text: The Emperor could use the good offices of the Kingdom of Italy in dealing with other powers, if he wished.

right.label: Italian version
right.text: The Emperor was obliged to conduct all foreign affairs through Italy, which treated Ethiopia as its protectorate.

slides.label: the Ethiopian army’s estimated advantage in numbers at Adwa
slides.text: Estimates for Menelik’s force range from 73,000 to over 100,000. Empress Taytu Betul marched with it and urged the 25,000-strong reserve into the fight.

events.text: Treaty of Wuchale, with its disputed Article 17
Battle of Adwa: the Italian army is routed
Treaty of Addis Ababa: Italy recognises Ethiopian independence
Adwa Victory Day is a public holiday across Ethiopia

slides.heading: Why it mattered
slides.text: During the Scramble for Africa, European powers carved up almost the whole continent. Ethiopia stayed independent, the only African country to owe its independence to a military victory, and historians count Adwa among the most notable reverses any European power suffered in that era.

slides.question: What did the two versions of the Treaty of Wuchale disagree about?
options: Who owned the port of Massawa
Whether Ethiopia must use Italy abroad
Where the border with Eritrea ran
slides.explanation: Article 17: the Amharic text said Ethiopia could use Italy’s good offices; the Italian text said it was obliged to, which Italy read as a protectorate.
